worst_places.quote: На push после squash-merge из пяти коммитов CI сравнит только с четырьмя из них уже проверенное состояние... и молча пропустит первый.

Это единственное место в зоне, где русский текст физически нечитаем; читатель вынужден идти в английскую версию, где мысль изложена ясно. Плюс здесь же впервые появляется squash-merge без пояснения.
worst_places.before: Обратная крайность — самодельный affected: `--base=HEAD~1`, "сравним с прошлым коммитом, чего мелочиться". На push после squash-merge из пяти коммитов CI сравнит только с четырьмя из них уже проверенное состояние... и молча пропустит первый.
worst_places.after: Обратная крайность — самодельный affected: `--base=HEAD~1`, "сравним с прошлым коммитом, чего мелочиться". Разберём push после squash-merge — когда пять коммитов ветки схлопнули в один. `HEAD~1` — это предыдущий коммит, а в нём уже учтены четыре изменения из пяти. worst_places.problem: 47 words, two colons and an em-dash aside in one breath; "severalfold" is a rare word a B1-B2 reader will not know, and "cold starts" is used here without ever being defined in the course. Chapter 06 EN is the most sentence-heavy file in the zone (25% over limit).
worst_places.before: The reflex "I'll make every lib buildable, like npm packages" is an expensive mistake: every lib grows a build config, the pipeline grows `^build` orchestration, cold starts slow down severalfold — and at ordinary repo sizes there's no payoff: vite builds the app from lib sources just fine.
worst_places.after: The reflex "I'll make every lib buildable, like npm packages" is an expensive mistake. At ordinary repo sizes there is no payoff in return: vite builds the app straight from the libs' sources just fine.

worst_places.after: Два термина из React-практики, на которых стоит эта матрица: **smart-компонент** сам добывает данные (запрос к API, чтение стора), **dumb-компонент** получает всё готовым через props и только рисует. worst_places.problem: 44 words with two parenthetical code asides and a semicolon splice, inside a 'Versions' callout the reader is meant to skim. The Russian version of the same callout is 36 words and reads noticeably lighter — the standard ~19% EN inflation pushes a borderline RU sentence well past the limit.
worst_places.before: Since Nx 18 the project path is taken as provided (`--directory=apps/shell` — literally that folder); in older versions (`projectNameAndRootFormat=derived`) Nx constructed the path itself from the name and nesting options, and the same command could put the project somewhere else.
worst_places.after: Since Nx 18 the project path is taken exactly as you provide it: `--directory=apps/shell` means literally that folder. Older versions behaved differently (`projectNameAndRootFormat=derived`): Nx built the path itself out of the project name and the nesting options. The same command could therefore drop the project somewhere else entirely.

patterns: The English version is systematically harder than the Russian one, and it is a length problem, not a vocabulary problem. RU keeps 3.5-10.5% of sentences over the limit; EN runs 12-26% on the very same chapters (ch00 24%, ch06 25%, ch07 26%). The cause is mechanical: the translator preserved the RU punctuation architecture — semicolon splice, colon, em-dash aside — while adding ~19% more words, so a controlled 38-word RU sentence becomes an uncontrolled 56-word EN one. Fix by splitting at the semicolons and colons that already mark the seams, not by cutting content.

Every chapter is disciplined about Nx's own vocabulary (target, task, executor, inputs, affected, tags are each defined at first use, in the chapter that owns them) and completely undisciplined about the surrounding industry vocabulary. CI appears 8-15 times per chapter and is never expanded anywhere in the first half; PR, SHA, e2e, AST, squash-merge, codemod, scaffolding, barrel, smart/dumb component, cold start all arrive as if already known. The rule the zone follows implicitly is 'explain what Nx invented, assume what the industry invented' — and the target reader is exactly the person who knows neither.

The 'Частая ошибка' / 'Common mistake' section is the single densest and longest-sentenced block in all 16 files. It always opens with the same 9-12 line paragraph shape ('Разработчик из single-app мира ...' / 'A developer from the single-app world ...') that packs the wrong reflex, its three consequences and the cure into one breath. It is also the most valuable section in each chapter, which is why it deserves the paragraph break most.

A small but repeating RU register slip: dev-slang lands mid-sentence where a neutral word was available — «в этом пойнт главы» (ch02), «тикет на выпил» (ch06), «структура репы уехала», «генерить прошлогоднюю структуру» (ch07). Individually charming, collectively they make the text harder for a reader whose Russian technical slang is thinner than the author's.
notes: Resembles `angular` (targeted-fixes), not `python-fullstack`: both locales are complete, idiomatic and independently authored — there is no Latin/Cyrillic hybrid-word layer here, and the RU reads as native writing, not translation. It falls short of angular's G 4.8 for two reasons only: the slang register above and one genuinely broken sentence in ru/05. Rubric E is the zone's strongest asset (4.9): every chapter opens its exercise with an explicit `Вход: workspace после главы NN`, and every code block carries its file path as the first comment line, so a reader returning after a week can restart from any chapter. Practice coverage is the real gap: the `nx` bank has 12 cards, all `junior`, and mapping them to this range gives ch00 (q1,2,9), ch01 (q3,7), ch02 (q5,11), ch03 (q4,10), ch04 (q8,12), ch07 (q6, dry-run only) — meaning **chapter 05 (affected) and chapter 06 (libs architecture, tags, module boundaries) have zero practice behind them**, and those are the two chapters the course itself calls its core value. The bank also writes `NX` where all 16 chapters write `Nx`. Chapter 06 specifically: judged on the 'assumed rather than taught' risk it holds up well — both axes are stated, tags are shown in project.json, the linter mechanics are traced through the graph, and the `'*' → '*'` placeholder trap is called out explicitly; its only real assumption is the smart/dumb component distinction (worst_places #6).
